title: Goulash
subtitle: Hungarian beef and paprika stew
excerpt: Hungary's defining dish: beef chuck braised low and slow in a paprika-rich sauce with onions, tomatoes, and caraway until the beef is falling-apart tender and the sauce is deep, sweet, and fragrant. Serve with egg noodles or bread dumplings.

recipe.sourceNotes: Goulash (gulyás in Hungarian, meaning herdsman) began as the food of Hungarian cattle drovers on the puszta, the great central plains, who cooked beef in paprika and onion in a cast-iron kettle (bogrács) over an open fire. The dish became a national symbol of Hungarian independence during the nineteenth century, promoted as the antithesis of Austrian Habsburg cuisine, and eventually spread across the Austro-Hungarian empire and beyond. Hungarian paprika is the critical ingredient: it should be good quality, sweet paprika, ideally from the regions around Kalocsa or Szeged. The dish can be made as a thick stew (pörkölt) or with additional stock to make a soup (gulyás leves). Outside Hungary, the term goulash is applied to many variations including the German dish with minced beef and pasta; the authentic form uses cubed beef and no flour for thickening.

content.text: Use sweet Hungarian paprika and use a lot of it: goulash is a paprika dish, not a beef stew with paprika in it. Remove the pan from the heat before adding the paprika; paprika scorches easily on a hot surface and turns bitter. Do not add flour; the stew thickens naturally as the collagen in the beef dissolves into the sauce over the long cooking time.

Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over high heat. Brown the beef in batches until deep golden on all sides. Remove and set aside. Reduce the heat to medium. Add all the onion and cook, stirring regularly, for 20 minutes until very soft and lightly golden; do not rush this. Add the garlic, caraway seeds, and red pepper and cook for 3 minutes.

Remove the pot from the heat. Add the paprika and stir quickly to combine with the onions. Return to low heat, add the tinned tomatoes and 400 ml water, and stir. Return the beef to the pot along with the bay leaves and salt. Stir well.

Cover and cook over very low heat for 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is completely tender and the sauce is thick and deep red. Taste and adjust the salt. Serve over egg noodles with soured cream if you like.
